practiceQuestions.stem: **[2.6 (2.6.2) — Function Transformation #22]** Let $f$ be a parent function analyzed in **2.6: Competing Function Model Validation** (*Competing Function Model Validation — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) such that the point $(2, 4)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$. If $g(x) = 3f(x - 2) + 5$, which point must lie on the graph of $y = g(x)$?
practiceQuestions.question: **[2.6 (2.6.2) — Function Transformation #22]** Let $f$ be a parent function analyzed in **2.6: Competing Function Model Validation** (*Competing Function Model Validation — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) such that the point $(2, 4)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$. If $g(x) = 3f(x - 2) + 5$, which point must lie on the graph of $y = g(x)$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
To use the known value $f(2) = 4$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:
$$x - 2 = 2 \implies x = 2 + 2 = 4$$
Then evaluate the output $g(4)$:
$$g(4) = 3f(2) + 5 = 3(4) + 5 = 17$$

**Exam Trap:** Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.

practiceQuestions.stem: **[2.6 (2.6.1) — Secant Line Approximation #23]** A smooth, continuous function $p(x)$ studied in **2.6: Competing Function Model Validation** (*Competing Function Model Validation — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) satisfies $p(3) = 6$ and $p(7) = 26$, and the graph of $p$ is strictly concave down on $[3, 7]$. Using the secant line connecting $(3, 6)$ and $(7, 26)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
practiceQuestions.question: **[2.6 (2.6.1) — Secant Line Approximation #23]** A smooth, continuous function $p(x)$ studied in **2.6: Competing Function Model Validation** (*Competing Function Model Validation — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) satisfies $p(3) = 6$ and $p(7) = 26$, and the graph of $p$ is strictly concave down on $[3, 7]$. Using the secant line connecting $(3, 6)$ and $(7, 26)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
choices: (A) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $26$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $16$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
options: (A) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $26$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $16$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Step 1: Compute the slope of the secant line on $[3, 7]$:
$$m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{p(7) - p(3)}{7 - 3} = \frac{26 - 6}{4} = 5$$
Step 2: Evaluate the secant line equation at $x = 4$:
$$L(4) = p(3) + m_{\text{sec}}(4 - 3) = 6 + 5(1) = 11$$
Step 3: Because $p$ is **concave down** on $[3, 7]$, the graph arches above the straight secant line connecting the endpoints, so the secant line lies below the curve and produces an **underestimate**.

**Exam Trap:** On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).

practiceQuestions.stem: **[2.6 (2.6.2) — Score-5 Synthesis Challenge #24]** Let $q(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 7$ be a function analyzed in **2.6: Competing Function Model Validation** (*Competing Function Model Validation — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*, governed by *Interpreting Asymptotes & Concavity in Physical Models*). If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $28$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
practiceQuestions.question: **[2.6 (2.6.2) — Score-5 Synthesis Challenge #24]** Let $q(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 7$ be a function analyzed in **2.6: Competing Function Model Validation** (*Competing Function Model Validation — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*, governed by *Interpreting Asymptotes & Concavity in Physical Models*). If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $28$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Using the algebraic difference quotient for a quadratic $q(x) = ax^2 + bx + d$ on $[1, c]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, c]} = \frac{q(c) - q(1)}{c - 1} = 4(c + 1) + 4$$
Setting this equal to $28$:
$$4(c + 1) + 4 = 28 \implies 4(c + 1) = 24 \implies c + 1 = 6 \implies c = 5$$

**Exam Trap:** When factoring $\frac{c^2 - 1^2}{c - 1} = c + 1$, remember not to drop the linear term $+4$ or forget to subtract $1$ in the final step.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: When factoring $\frac{c^2 - 1^2}{c - 1} = c + 1$, remember not to drop the linear term $+4$ or forget to subtract $1$ in the final step.

topics.title: Composition of Functions
topics.summary: Function composition chains two processes together: first $x \mapsto g(x)$, and then $g(x) \mapsto f(g(x))$. Crucial to AP Precalculus is determining the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ BEFORE algebraically simplifying radicals or fractions—any restriction from the inner function $g(x)$ remains in force even if algebraically canceled later. Mastering **2.7A (Composition of Functions)** matters because it gives you the direct mathematical rule needed to set up, evaluate, and interpret AP Precalculus multiple-choice and free-response questions without guesswork.

lesson.concept_description: Function composition chains two processes together: first $x \mapsto g(x)$, and then $g(x) \mapsto f(g(x))$. Crucial to AP Precalculus is determining the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ BEFORE algebraically simplifying radicals or fractions—any restriction from the inner function $g(x)$ remains in force even if algebraically canceled later. Mastering **2.7A (Composition of Functions)** matters because it gives you the direct mathematical rule needed to set up, evaluate, and interpret AP Precalculus multiple-choice and free-response questions without guesswork.
lesson.core_formula:
**Composite Function Definition (2.7A.1):**
$$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** The output of the inner function $g(x)$ becomes the input to the outer function $f$.

**Domain of a Composite Function (2.7A.1):**
$$\text{Dom}(f \circ g) = \{x \in \text{Dom}(g) \mid g(x) \in \text{Dom}(f)\}$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** $x$ must be in the domain of the inner function $g$, AND $g(x)$ must lie in the domain of the outer function $f$.
lesson.simple_explanation:
**Intuitive Analogy:** Think of exponential growth like a snowball rolling downhill that multiplies by the same factor $b$ on every equal step $\Delta x$, while a logarithm works in reverse by asking: "How many times did we multiply by base $b$ to reach this output?"

**How to Apply the Formula:**
1. **Preserving Inner Domain Restrictions:** If $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$, the algebraic simplification of $f(g(x)) = (\sqrt{x - 3})^2 + 1 = x - 2$ still has domain $x \ge 3$ because $g(x)$ is undefined for $x < 3$.

**Quick Application Example:**
Find the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ where $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}$ and $g(x) = x^2$.
- Step 1: The domain of the inner function $g(x) = x^2$ is $(-\infty, \infty)$. The domain of $f(u) = \sqrt{4 - u}$ requires $4 - u \ge 0 \implies u \le 4$.
- Step 2: Substitute $u = g(x) = x^2$: we require $x^2 \le 4$.
- Step 3: Solve $x^2 \le 4 \implies -2 \le x \le 2$, so the domain is $[-2, 2]$.

practiceQuestions.question:
**[2.7A (2.7A.1) — Tabular Analysis #1]** Selected values of a function $f$ analyzed in *Composition of Functions* (*Composition of Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) are given in the table below:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 1 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\ \hline f(x) & 3 & 9 & 17 & 33 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
What is the average rate of change of $f$ over the closed interval $[1, 7]$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Using the average rate of change (difference quotient) formula over $[1, 7]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, 7]} = \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = \frac{30}{6} = 5$$

**Exam Trap:** Do not stop after finding the net change $\Delta f = 30$ (which omits division by $\Delta x = 6$), and never invert the difference quotient as $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}$.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: Do not stop after finding the net change $\Delta f = 30$ (which omits division by $\Delta x = 6$), and never invert the difference quotient as $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}$.

practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7A (2.7A.2) — Graphical Behavior #2]** On the open interval $(2, 7)$, the graph of a smooth function $g$ modeling *Composition of Functions* (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) is strictly decreasing and concave up. Which of the following statements about $g$ and its average rate of change over equal-length subintervals of $(2, 7)$ MUST be true?
choices: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
options: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Because $g$ is decreasing on $(2, 7)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).

**Exam Trap:** Confusing "negative and increasing" (e.g., $-6 < -3 < -1$, concave up) with "negative and becoming steeper" (which is decreasing, e.g., $-1 > -3 > -6$, concave down).

practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7A (2.7A.2) — Parameter Synthesis #4]** Let $h(x) = k x^2 + 6$ be a parameterized model studied in **2.7A: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*), where $k$ is a real constant. If $h(2) = 26$, what is the value of the parameter $k$, and what is the average rate of change of $h$ on $[0, 2]$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
First solve for $k$ using $h(2) = 26$:
$$k(2)^2 + 6 = 26 \implies 4k = 20 \implies k = 5$$
Next, compute the average rate of change on $[0, 2]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,2]} = \frac{h(2) - h(0)}{2 - 0} = \frac{26 - 6}{2} = \frac{20}{2} = 10$$

**Exam Trap:** Forgetting to square the input $x = 2$ when solving $k(2)^2 = 20$, or forgetting to divide the net change $h(2) - h(0) = 20$ by the interval length $\Delta x = 2$.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: Forgetting to square the input $x = 2$ when solving $k(2)^2 = 20$, or forgetting to divide the net change $h(2) - h(0) = 20$ by the interval length $\Delta x = 2$.

Using a graphing calculator, what is the value of $M(4)$ and the average rate of change of $M$ over the interval $[0, 4]$, rounded to three decimal places?
practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7A (2.7A.1) — Calculator-Active Modeling #5]** A quantity studied in **2.7A: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) is modeled by the function $M(t) = 140(1.12)^t$ for $t \ge 0$ hours. Using a graphing calculator, what is the value of $M(4)$ and the average rate of change of $M$ over the interval $[0, 4]$, rounded to three decimal places?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Evaluating $M(4)$ directly on a graphing calculator without intermediate rounding:
$$M(4) = 140(1.12)^{4} \approx 220.293$$
Since $M(0) = 140(1.12)^0 = 140$, the average rate of change on $[0, 4]$ is:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,4]} = \frac{M(4) - M(0)}{4 - 0} = \frac{220.293 - 140}{4} \approx 20.073$$

**Exam Trap:** Never assume $M(0) = 0$ for an exponential model $M(t) = a \cdot b^t$ (since $b^0 = 1$, $M(0) = 140$), and always divide the net change by $\Delta t = 4$.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: Never assume $M(0) = 0$ for an exponential model $M(t) = a \cdot b^t$ (since $b^0 = 1$, $M(0) = 140$), and always divide the net change by $\Delta t = 4$.

practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7A (2.7A.2) — Function Transformation #6]** Let $f$ be a parent function analyzed in **2.7A: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) such that the point $(2, 3)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$. If $g(x) = 3f(x - 1) + 7$, which point must lie on the graph of $y = g(x)$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
To use the known value $f(2) = 3$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:
$$x - 1 = 2 \implies x = 2 + 1 = 3$$
Then evaluate the output $g(3)$:
$$g(3) = 3f(2) + 7 = 3(3) + 7 = 16$$

**Exam Trap:** Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.

practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7A (2.7A.1) — Secant Line Approximation #7]** A smooth, continuous function $p(x)$ studied in **2.7A: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) satisfies $p(3) = 5$ and $p(7) = 25$, and the graph of $p$ is strictly concave down on $[3, 7]$. Using the secant line connecting $(3, 5)$ and $(7, 25)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
choices: (A) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $25$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $15$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
options: (A) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $25$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $15$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Step 1: Compute the slope of the secant line on $[3, 7]$:
$$m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{p(7) - p(3)}{7 - 3} = \frac{25 - 5}{4} = 5$$
Step 2: Evaluate the secant line equation at $x = 4$:
$$L(4) = p(3) + m_{\text{sec}}(4 - 3) = 5 + 5(1) = 10$$
Step 3: Because $p$ is **concave down** on $[3, 7]$, the graph arches above the straight secant line connecting the endpoints, so the secant line lies below the curve and produces an **underestimate**.

**Exam Trap:** On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).

practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7A (2.7A.2) — Score-5 Synthesis Challenge #8]** Let $q(x) = 3x^2 + 4x - 7$ be a function analyzed in **2.7A: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*, governed by *Preserving Inner Domain Restrictions*). If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $19$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Using the algebraic difference quotient for a quadratic $q(x) = ax^2 + bx + d$ on $[1, c]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, c]} = \frac{q(c) - q(1)}{c - 1} = 3(c + 1) + 4$$
Setting this equal to $19$:
$$3(c + 1) + 4 = 19 \implies 3(c + 1) = 15 \implies c + 1 = 5 \implies c = 4$$

**Exam Trap:** When factoring $\frac{c^2 - 1^2}{c - 1} = c + 1$, remember not to drop the linear term $+4$ or forget to subtract $1$ in the final step.
practiceQuestions.trapExplanation: When factoring $\frac{c^2 - 1^2}{c - 1} = c + 1$, remember not to drop the linear term $+4$ or forget to subtract $1$ in the final step.

topics.title: Composition of Functions
topics.summary: Function composition chains two processes together: first $x \mapsto g(x)$, and then $g(x) \mapsto f(g(x))$. Crucial to AP Precalculus is determining the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ BEFORE algebraically simplifying radicals or fractions—any restriction from the inner function $g(x)$ remains in force even if algebraically canceled later. Mastering **2.7B (Composition of Functions)** matters because it gives you the direct mathematical rule needed to set up, evaluate, and interpret AP Precalculus multiple-choice and free-response questions without guesswork.

lesson.core_formula:
**Composite Function Definition (2.7B.1):**
$$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** The output of the inner function $g(x)$ becomes the input to the outer function $f$.

**Domain of a Composite Function (2.7B.1):**
$$\text{Dom}(f \circ g) = \{x \in \text{Dom}(g) \mid g(x) \in \text{Dom}(f)\}$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** $x$ must be in the domain of the inner function $g$, AND $g(x)$ must lie in the domain of the outer function $f$.
lesson.simple_explanation:
**Intuitive Analogy:** Think of exponential growth like a snowball rolling downhill that multiplies by the same factor $b$ on every equal step $\Delta x$, while a logarithm works in reverse by asking: "How many times did we multiply by base $b$ to reach this output?"

**How to Apply the Formula:**
1. **Preserving Inner Domain Restrictions:** If $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$, the algebraic simplification of $f(g(x)) = (\sqrt{x - 3})^2 + 1 = x - 2$ still has domain $x \ge 3$ because $g(x)$ is undefined for $x < 3$.

**Quick Application Example:**
Find the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ where $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}$ and $g(x) = x^2$.
- Step 1: The domain of the inner function $g(x) = x^2$ is $(-\infty, \infty)$. The domain of $f(u) = \sqrt{4 - u}$ requires $4 - u \ge 0 \implies u \le 4$.
- Step 2: Substitute $u = g(x) = x^2$: we require $x^2 \le 4$.
- Step 3: Solve $x^2 \le 4 \implies -2 \le x \le 2$, so the domain is $[-2, 2]$.

1. **Preserving Inner Domain Restrictions:** If $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$, the algebraic simplification of $f(g(x)) = (\sqrt{x - 3})^2 + 1 = x - 2$ still has domain $x \ge 3$ because $g(x)$ is undefined for $x < 3$.

**Quick Application Example:**
Find the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ where $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}$ and $g(x) = x^2$.
- Step 1: The domain of the inner function $g(x) = x^2$ is $(-\infty, \infty)$. The domain of $f(u) = \sqrt{4 - u}$ requires $4 - u \ge 0 \implies u \le 4$.
- Step 2: Substitute $u = g(x) = x^2$: we require $x^2 \le 4$.
- Step 3: Solve $x^2 \le 4 \implies -2 \le x \le 2$, so the domain is $[-2, 2]$.

master_lesson.core_formula:
**Composite Function Definition (2.7B.1):**
$$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$$

- **Variables & Meaning:** $x$ must be in the domain of the inner function $g$, AND $g(x)$ must lie in the domain of the outer function $f$.

mcq.question_latex:
**[2.7B (2.7B.1) — Tabular Analysis #1]** Selected values of a function $f$ analyzed in *Composition of Functions* (*Composition of Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) are given in the table below:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 1 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\ \hline f(x) & 3 & 9 & 17 & 33 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
What is the average rate of change of $f$ over the closed interval $[1, 7]$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Using the average rate of change (difference quotient) formula over $[1, 7]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, 7]} = \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = \frac{30}{6} = 5$$
mcq.exam_trap: Do not stop after finding the net change $\Delta f = 30$ (which omits division by $\Delta x = 6$), and never invert the difference quotient as $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Computed only the numerator net change $\Delta f = f(7) - f(1) = 33 - 3 = 30$ and forgot to divide by the interval width $\Delta x = 7 - 1 = 6$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the rate of change over the interior subinterval $[3, 5]$ ($\frac{17 - 9}{5 - 3} = 4$) instead of using the endpoints $x = 1$ and $x = 7$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Correct! Uses the difference quotient $\frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = 5$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Inverted the slope formula by computing $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} = \frac{6}{30} \approx 0.2$ instead of $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.7B (2.7B.2) — Graphical Behavior #2]** On the open interval $(2, 7)$, the graph of a smooth function $g$ modeling *Composition of Functions* (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) is strictly decreasing and concave up. Which of the following statements about $g$ and its average rate of change over equal-length subintervals of $(2, 7)$ MUST be true?
options: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
mcq.explanation_latex: Because $g$ is decreasing on $(2, 7)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).
mcq.exam_trap: Confusing "negative and increasing" (e.g., $-6 < -3 < -1$, concave up) with "negative and becoming steeper" (which is decreasing, e.g., $-1 > -3 > -6$, concave down).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Looked at the magnitude of the negative slopes rather than their signed values. Moving from $-8$ to $-4$ to $-1$ is an INCREASING rate of change (concave up), whereas negative and decreasing ($-1, -4, -8$) is concave down.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Reversed the direction of $g(x)$. The prompt states $g$ is strictly decreasing.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Assumed "concave up" means positive slopes. A decreasing concave-up curve has negative slopes that are becoming less steep.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Decreasing function means negative rates of change, and concave up means the rates of change are increasing (becoming less negative, e.g., $-8, -4, -1$).

mcq.question_latex: **[2.7B (2.7B.2) — Parameter Synthesis #4]** Let $h(x) = k x^2 + 6$ be a parameterized model studied in **2.7B: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*), where $k$ is a real constant. If $h(2) = 26$, what is the value of the parameter $k$, and what is the average rate of change of $h$ on $[0, 2]$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
First solve for $k$ using $h(2) = 26$:
$$k(2)^2 + 6 = 26 \implies 4k = 20 \implies k = 5$$
Next, compute the average rate of change on $[0, 2]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,2]} = \frac{h(2) - h(0)}{2 - 0} = \frac{26 - 6}{2} = \frac{20}{2} = 10$$

distractor_diagnostics.B: Correct! Isolating $k$ gives $k(2)^2 = 20 \implies k = 5$, and $\text{AROC}_{[0,2]} = \frac{26 - 6}{2 - 0} = 10$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Divided 20 by $2$ instead of $2^2 = 4$ when solving $k(2)^2 + 6 = 26$ for $k$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Forgot to divide by $2^2 = 4$ when isolating $k$, and used $h(2) = 26$ as the rate of change without subtracting $h(0) = 6$.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.7B (2.7B.1) — Calculator-Active Modeling #5]** A quantity studied in **2.7B: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) is modeled by the function $M(t) = 140(1.12)^t$ for $t \ge 0$ hours. mcq.question_latex: **[2.7B (2.7B.2) — Function Transformation #6]** Let $f$ be a parent function analyzed in **2.7B: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) such that the point $(2, 3)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$. If $g(x) = 3f(x - 1) + 7$, which point must lie on the graph of $y = g(x)$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
To use the known value $f(2) = 3$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:
$$x - 1 = 2 \implies x = 2 + 1 = 3$$
Then evaluate the output $g(3)$:
$$g(3) = 3f(2) + 7 = 3(3) + 7 = 16$$
mcq.exam_trap: Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Subtracted $1$ from the $x$-coordinate instead of adding $1$. Remember that $f(x - 1)$ shifts the graph RIGHT by $1$ units ($x - 1 = 2 \implies x = 3$).
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Added the vertical shift $+7$ BEFORE multiplying by the vertical stretch factor $3$. By order of operations, multiply $3 \cdot 3$ first, then add $7$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Applied the vertical stretch factor $3$ to the $x$-coordinate instead of the $y$-coordinate.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Setting $x - 1 = 2$ gives $x = 3$ (horizontal shift right by $1$), and $g(3) = 3f(2) + 7 = 3(3) + 7 = 16$.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.7B (2.7B.1) — Secant Line Approximation #7]** A smooth, continuous function $p(x)$ studied in **2.7B: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) satisfies $p(3) = 5$ and $p(7) = 25$, and the graph of $p$ is strictly concave down on $[3, 7]$. Using the secant line connecting $(3, 5)$ and $(7, 25)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
options: (A) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $25$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $15$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
mcq.explanation_latex:
Step 1: Compute the slope of the secant line on $[3, 7]$:
$$m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{p(7) - p(3)}{7 - 3} = \frac{25 - 5}{4} = 5$$
Step 2: Evaluate the secant line equation at $x = 4$:
$$L(4) = p(3) + m_{\text{sec}}(4 - 3) = 5 + 5(1) = 10$$
Step 3: Because $p$ is **concave down** on $[3, 7]$, the graph arches above the straight secant line connecting the endpoints, so the secant line lies below the curve and produces an **underestimate**.
mcq.exam_trap: On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct! The secant slope is $m = \frac{25 - 5}{7 - 3} = 5$, giving $L(4) = 5 + 5(4 - 3) = 10$. For a concave-down curve, the straight secant line connecting two points lies below the curve on $(3, 7)$, yielding an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the secant approximation $10$ properly, but reversed the concavity rule! Because a concave-down curve arches upward like an umbrella, the straight line connecting two points on the curve sits underneath the curve and gives an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Used $L(x) = 5 + 5x$ instead of point-slope form $L(x) = 5 + 5(x - 3)$ (forgot to subtract $x_1 = 3$).
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Averaged the endpoint outputs $\frac{5 + 25}{2}$ even though $x = 4$ is not the midpoint of $[3, 7]$, and reversed the secant concavity inequality.

distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Subtracted the linear coefficient $4$ from $19$, but forgot to divide by the leading coefficient $a = 3$ and subtract $1$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct! The secant slope is $m = \frac{26 - 6}{7 - 3} = 5$, giving $L(4) = 6 + 5(4 - 3) = 11$. For a concave-down curve, the straight secant line connecting two points lies below the curve on $(3, 7)$, yielding an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the secant approximation $11$ properly, but reversed the concavity rule! Because a concave-down curve arches upward like an umbrella, the straight line connecting two points on the curve sits underneath the curve and gives an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Used $L(x) = 6 + 5x$ instead of point-slope form $L(x) = 6 + 5(x - 3)$ (forgot to subtract $x_1 = 3$).

choices: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
options: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.

Because $g$ is decreasing on $(2, 7)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).

practiceQuestions.explanation:
To use the known value $f(2) = 4$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:
$$x - 2 = 2 \implies x = 2 + 2 = 4$$
Then evaluate the output $g(4)$:
$$g(4) = 3f(2) + 5 = 3(4) + 5 = 17$$

Using the secant line connecting $(3, 6)$ and $(7, 26)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
choices: (A) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $26$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $16$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.

practiceQuestions.explanation:
Step 1: Compute the slope of the secant line on $[3, 7]$:
$$m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{p(7) - p(3)}{7 - 3} = \frac{26 - 6}{4} = 5$$
Step 2: Evaluate the secant line equation at $x = 4$:
$$L(4) = p(3) + m_{\text{sec}}(4 - 3) = 6 + 5(1) = 11$$
Step 3: Because $p$ is **concave down** on $[3, 7]$, the graph arches above the straight secant line connecting the endpoints, so the secant line lies below the curve and produces an **underestimate**.

**Exam Trap:** On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).

practiceQuestions.question: **[2.7B (2.7B.2) — Score-5 Synthesis Challenge #24]** Let $q(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 7$ be a function analyzed in **2.7B: Composition of Functions** (*Composition of Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*, governed by *Preserving Inner Domain Restrictions*). If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $28$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Using the algebraic difference quotient for a quadratic $q(x) = ax^2 + bx + d$ on $[1, c]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, c]} = \frac{q(c) - q(1)}{c - 1} = 4(c + 1) + 4$$
Setting this equal to $28$:
$$4(c + 1) + 4 = 28 \implies 4(c + 1) = 24 \implies c + 1 = 6 \implies c = 5$$

topics.title: Inverse Functions
topics.summary: A function $f$ has an inverse function $f^{-1}$ on its domain if and only if $f$ is **one-to-one** (injective)—meaning every output value corresponds to a unique input value, or equivalently its graph passes the **Horizontal Line Test**. Any strictly increasing or strictly decreasing function on an interval is invertible on that interval. Mastering **2.8 (Inverse Functions)** matters because it gives you the direct mathematical rule needed to set up, evaluate, and interpret AP Precalculus multiple-choice and free-response questions without guesswork.

lesson.concept_description: A function $f$ has an inverse function $f^{-1}$ on its domain if and only if $f$ is **one-to-one** (injective)—meaning every output value corresponds to a unique input value, or equivalently its graph passes the **Horizontal Line Test**. Any strictly increasing or strictly decreasing function on an interval is invertible on that interval. Mastering **2.8 (Inverse Functions)** matters because it gives you the direct mathematical rule needed to set up, evaluate, and interpret AP Precalculus multiple-choice and free-response questions without guesswork.
lesson.core_formula:
**Inverse Equivalence & Composition Identity (2.8.1):**
$$f(a) = b \iff f^{-1}(b) = a; \quad f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \text{ and } f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** The inverse function reverses input and output roles.

**Domain and Range Symmetry (2.8.1):**
$$\text{Dom}(f^{-1}) = \text{Ran}(f), \quad \text{Ran}(f^{-1}) = \text{Dom}(f)$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** The graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of $y = f(x)$ across the line $y = x$.
lesson.simple_explanation:
**Intuitive Analogy:** Think of exponential growth like a snowball rolling downhill that multiplies by the same factor $b$ on every equal step $\Delta x$, while a logarithm works in reverse by asking: "How many times did we multiply by base $b$ to reach this output?"

**How to Apply the Formula:**
1. **Inheriting Domain Restrictions on $f^{-1}(x)$:** When inverting a function with a restricted range, such as $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 7} + 1$ (which has domain $x \ge 7$ and range $y \ge 1$), the algebraic inverse $f^{-1}(x) = (x - 1)^2 + 7$ MUST include the inherited domain restriction $x \ge 1$ so that $f^{-1}$ remains one-to-one.

**Quick Application Example:**
Find the equation and domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ for $f(x) = \frac{2x + 3}{x - 4}$.
- Step 1: Swap $x$ and $y$: $x = \frac{2y + 3}{y - 4}$.
- Step 2: Multiply by $(y - 4)$ and collect $y$ terms: $xy - 4x = 2y + 3 \implies y(x - 2) = 4x + 3$.
- Step 3: Divide by $(x - 2)$: $f^{-1}(x) = \frac{4x + 3}{x - 2}$ with domain $x \ne 2$ (which matches the horizontal asymptote $y = 2$ of $f$).

mcq.question_latex: What is the inverse of the function $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 7} + 1$?
mcq.explanation_latex: Since $\sqrt{x-7} \ge 0$, the range of $f$ is $[1, \infty)$. Swapping $x$ and $y$ in $y = \sqrt{x-7} + 1$ gives $x - 1 = \sqrt{y - 7} \implies y = (x - 1)^2 + 7$ with inherited domain $x \ge 1$.

distractor_diagnostics.C: Selecting (C) $f^{-1}(x) = (x + 1)^2 - 7$ for $x \ge 7$ triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Omitting the domain restriction $x \ge 1$ (Option A), which includes the extraneous left half of the parabola.

options: (A) $f$ has an inverse function because every input has one output.

mcq.question_latex: If $f$ is a one-to-one function such that $f(5) = -12$ and the average rate of change of $f$ on $[2, 5]$ is $-3$, what is the average rate of change of $f^{-1}$ on $[-12, -3]$?
mcq.explanation_latex: Since AROC of $f$ on $[2, 5]$ is $-3$, $\frac{f(5) - f(2)}{5 - 2} = -3 \implies -12 - f(2) = -9 \implies f(2) = -3$. Thus $(2, -3)$ and $(5, -12)$ are on $f$, so $(-3, 2)$ and $(-12, 5)$ are on $f^{-1}$. The slope between them is $\frac{2 - 5}{-3 - (-12)} = -\frac{3}{9} = -\frac{1}{3}$ (the reciprocal of the slope of $f$).

mcq.question_latex:
**[2.8 (2.8.1) — Tabular Analysis #1]** Selected values of a function $f$ analyzed in *Inverse Functions* (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) are given in the table below:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 1 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\ \hline f(x) & 3 & 9 & 17 & 33 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
What is the average rate of change of $f$ over the closed interval $[1, 7]$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Using the average rate of change (difference quotient) formula over $[1, 7]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, 7]} = \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = \frac{30}{6} = 5$$
mcq.exam_trap: Do not stop after finding the net change $\Delta f = 30$ (which omits division by $\Delta x = 6$), and never invert the difference quotient as $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Computed only the numerator net change $\Delta f = f(7) - f(1) = 33 - 3 = 30$ and forgot to divide by the interval width $\Delta x = 7 - 1 = 6$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the rate of change over the interior subinterval $[3, 5]$ ($\frac{17 - 9}{5 - 3} = 4$) instead of using the endpoints $x = 1$ and $x = 7$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Correct! Uses the difference quotient $\frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = 5$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Inverted the slope formula by computing $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} = \frac{6}{30} \approx 0.2$ instead of $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.2) — Graphical Behavior #2]** On the open interval $(2, 7)$, the graph of a smooth function $g$ modeling *Inverse Functions* (*Inverse Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) is strictly decreasing and concave up. Which of the following statements about $g$ and its average rate of change over equal-length subintervals of $(2, 7)$ MUST be true?
options: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
mcq.explanation_latex: Because $g$ is decreasing on $(2, 7)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).
mcq.exam_trap: Confusing "negative and increasing" (e.g., $-6 < -3 < -1$, concave up) with "negative and becoming steeper" (which is decreasing, e.g., $-1 > -3 > -6$, concave down).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Looked at the magnitude of the negative slopes rather than their signed values. Moving from $-8$ to $-4$ to $-1$ is an INCREASING rate of change (concave up), whereas negative and decreasing ($-1, -4, -8$) is concave down.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Reversed the direction of $g(x)$. The prompt states $g$ is strictly decreasing.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Assumed "concave up" means positive slopes. A decreasing concave-up curve has negative slopes that are becoming less steep.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Decreasing function means negative rates of change, and concave up means the rates of change are increasing (becoming less negative, e.g., $-8, -4, -1$).

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.2) — Graphical Behavior #18]** On the open interval $(4, 9)$, the graph of a smooth function $g$ modeling *Inverse Functions* (*Inverse Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) is strictly decreasing and concave up. Which of the following statements about $g$ and its average rate of change over equal-length subintervals of $(4, 9)$ MUST be true?
options: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
mcq.explanation_latex: Because $g$ is decreasing on $(4, 9)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).
mcq.exam_trap: Confusing "negative and increasing" (e.g., $-6 < -3 < -1$, concave up) with "negative and becoming steeper" (which is decreasing, e.g., $-1 > -3 > -6$, concave down).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Looked at the magnitude of the negative slopes rather than their signed values. Moving from $-8$ to $-4$ to $-1$ is an INCREASING rate of change (concave up), whereas negative and decreasing ($-1, -4, -8$) is concave down.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Reversed the direction of $g(x)$. The prompt states $g$ is strictly decreasing.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Assumed "concave up" means positive slopes. A decreasing concave-up curve has negative slopes that are becoming less steep.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Decreasing function means negative rates of change, and concave up means the rates of change are increasing (becoming less negative, e.g., $-8, -4, -1$).

**[2.8 (2.8.1) — Foundational Formula Use #19]** In the analysis of **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*), the governing mathematical relationship is given by **Inverse Equivalence & Composition Identity**:
$$f(a) = b \iff f^{-1}(b) = a; \quad f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \text{ and } f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$$
Which of the following best describes the mathematical role and domain condition of this identity?
options: (A) The inverse function reverses input and output roles.
(B) It holds only when the average rate of change is identically zero over all real numbers.
(C) It requires the independent variable to be restricted exclusively to negative integers.
(D) It implies that the graph has a removable discontinuity (hole) at every integer input.
mcq.explanation_latex: By the AP Precalculus specifications for **2.8 (2.8.1)**, **Inverse Equivalence & Composition Identity** ($f(a) = b \iff f^{-1}(b) = a; \quad f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \text{ and } f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$) satisfies: The inverse function reverses input and output roles.
mcq.exam_trap: Overlooking explicit domain exclusions or confusing structural identities with constant-rate conditions.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct! Directly reflects the official AP Precalculus specification and domain condition for Inverse Equivalence & Composition Identity in 2.8.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Assumed a zero rate of change (constant function), which contradicts how Inverse Equivalence & Composition Identity models dynamic covariation in Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Imposed an artificial negative-integer domain restriction not present in f(a) = b \iff f^{-1}(b) = a; \quad f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \text{ and } f^{-1}(f(x)) = x.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Confused standard functional evaluation in Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations with removable rational discontinuities (holes) at integer inputs.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.2) — Parameter Synthesis #20]** Let $h(x) = k x^2 + 7$ be a parameterized model studied in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*), where $k$ is a real constant. If $h(3) = 70$, what is the value of the parameter $k$, and what is the average rate of change of $h$ on $[0, 3]$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
First solve for $k$ using $h(3) = 70$:
$$k(3)^2 + 7 = 70 \implies 9k = 63 \implies k = 7$$
Next, compute the average rate of change on $[0, 3]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,3]} = \frac{h(3) - h(0)}{3 - 0} = \frac{70 - 7}{3} = \frac{63}{3} = 21$$
mcq.exam_trap: Forgetting to square the input $x = 3$ when solving $k(3)^2 = 63$, or forgetting to divide the net change $h(3) - h(0) = 63$ by the interval length $\Delta x = 3$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Found $k = 7$ correctly, but reported the net change $h(3) - h(0) = 63$ instead of dividing by the interval width $\Delta x = 3 - 0 = 3$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Correct! Isolating $k$ gives $k(3)^2 = 63 \implies k = 7$, and $\text{AROC}_{[0,3]} = \frac{70 - 7}{3 - 0} = 21$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Divided 63 by $3$ instead of $3^2 = 9$ when solving $k(3)^2 + 7 = 70$ for $k$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Forgot to divide by $3^2 = 9$ when isolating $k$, and used $h(3) = 70$ as the rate of change without subtracting $h(0) = 7$.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.1) — Calculator-Active Modeling #21]** A quantity studied in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) is modeled by the function $M(t) = 120(1.12)^t$ for $t \ge 0$ hours. Using a graphing calculator, what is the value of $M(5)$ and the average rate of change of $M$ over the interval $[0, 5]$, rounded to three decimal places?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Evaluating $M(5)$ directly on a graphing calculator without intermediate rounding:
$$M(5) = 120(1.12)^{5} \approx 211.481$$
Since $M(0) = 120(1.12)^0 = 120$, the average rate of change on $[0, 5]$ is:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,5]} = \frac{M(5) - M(0)}{5 - 0} = \frac{211.481 - 120}{5} \approx 18.296$$
mcq.exam_trap: Never assume $M(0) = 0$ for an exponential model $M(t) = a \cdot b^t$ (since $b^0 = 1$, $M(0) = 120$), and always divide the net change by $\Delta t = 5$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Computed $M(5) \approx 211.481$ and subtracted $M(0) = 120$ to get $91.481$, but forgot to divide by the time interval $\Delta t = 5$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Treated the exponential power $(1.12)^{5}$ as multiplication 120 \cdot 1.12 \cdot 5 instead of exponentiation.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Divided $M(5)$ by $5$ without subtracting the initial value $M(0) = 120$ in the numerator (assuming $M(0) = 0$ when $(1.12)^0 = 1$).

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.2) — Function Transformation #22]** Let $f$ be a parent function analyzed in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) such that the point $(2, 4)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$. If $g(x) = 3f(x - 2) + 5$, which point must lie on the graph of $y = g(x)$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
To use the known value $f(2) = 4$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:
$$x - 2 = 2 \implies x = 2 + 2 = 4$$
Then evaluate the output $g(4)$:
$$g(4) = 3f(2) + 5 = 3(4) + 5 = 17$$
mcq.exam_trap: Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Subtracted $2$ from the $x$-coordinate instead of adding $2$. Remember that $f(x - 2)$ shifts the graph RIGHT by $2$ units ($x - 2 = 2 \implies x = 4$).
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Added the vertical shift $+5$ BEFORE multiplying by the vertical stretch factor $3$. By order of operations, multiply $3 \cdot 4$ first, then add $5$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Applied the vertical stretch factor $3$ to the $x$-coordinate instead of the $y$-coordinate.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Setting $x - 2 = 2$ gives $x = 4$ (horizontal shift right by $2$), and $g(4) = 3f(2) + 5 = 3(4) + 5 = 17$.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.1) — Secant Line Approximation #23]** A smooth, continuous function $p(x)$ studied in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) satisfies $p(3) = 6$ and $p(7) = 26$, and the graph of $p$ is strictly concave down on $[3, 7]$. Using the secant line connecting $(3, 6)$ and $(7, 26)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
options: (A) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $11$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $26$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $16$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
mcq.explanation_latex:
Step 1: Compute the slope of the secant line on $[3, 7]$:
$$m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{p(7) - p(3)}{7 - 3} = \frac{26 - 6}{4} = 5$$
Step 2: Evaluate the secant line equation at $x = 4$:
$$L(4) = p(3) + m_{\text{sec}}(4 - 3) = 6 + 5(1) = 11$$
Step 3: Because $p$ is **concave down** on $[3, 7]$, the graph arches above the straight secant line connecting the endpoints, so the secant line lies below the curve and produces an **underestimate**.
mcq.exam_trap: On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct! The secant slope is $m = \frac{26 - 6}{7 - 3} = 5$, giving $L(4) = 6 + 5(4 - 3) = 11$. For a concave-down curve, the straight secant line connecting two points lies below the curve on $(3, 7)$, yielding an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the secant approximation $11$ properly, but reversed the concavity rule! Because a concave-down curve arches upward like an umbrella, the straight line connecting two points on the curve sits underneath the curve and gives an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Used $L(x) = 6 + 5x$ instead of point-slope form $L(x) = 6 + 5(x - 3)$ (forgot to subtract $x_1 = 3$).
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Averaged the endpoint outputs $\frac{6 + 26}{2}$ even though $x = 4$ is not the midpoint of $[3, 7]$, and reversed the secant concavity inequality.

mcq.question_latex: **[2.8 (2.8.2) — Score-5 Synthesis Challenge #24]** Let $q(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 7$ be a function analyzed in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*, governed by *Inheriting Domain Restrictions on $f^{-1}(x)$*). If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $28$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Using the algebraic difference quotient for a quadratic $q(x) = ax^2 + bx + d$ on $[1, c]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, c]} = \frac{q(c) - q(1)}{c - 1} = 4(c + 1) + 4$$
Setting this equal to $28$:
$$4(c + 1) + 4 = 28 \implies 4(c + 1) = 24 \implies c + 1 = 6 \implies c = 5$$
mcq.exam_trap: When factoring $\frac{c^2 - 1^2}{c - 1} = c + 1$, remember not to drop the linear term $+4$ or forget to subtract $1$ in the final step.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Solved properly for $(1 + c) = 6$, but forgot to subtract the left endpoint $x_1 = 1$ to isolate $c$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Correct! For $q(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 7$, the difference quotient on $[1, c]$ simplifies to $\text{AROC} = 4(1 + c) + 4$. Setting 4(1 + c) + 4 = 28 yields $c = 5$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Subtracted the linear coefficient $4$ from $28$, but forgot to divide by the leading coefficient $a = 4$ and subtract $1$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Confused the average rate of change with the total change $q(5) - q(1) = 112$.

practiceQuestions.stem: If $f$ is a one-to-one function such that $f(5) = -12$ and the average rate of change of $f$ on $[2, 5]$ is $-3$, what is the average rate of change of $f^{-1}$ on $[-12, -3]$?
practiceQuestions.question: If $f$ is a one-to-one function such that $f(5) = -12$ and the average rate of change of $f$ on $[2, 5]$ is $-3$, what is the average rate of change of $f^{-1}$ on $[-12, -3]$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Since AROC of $f$ on $[2, 5]$ is $-3$, $\frac{f(5) - f(2)}{5 - 2} = -3 \implies -12 - f(2) = -9 \implies f(2) = -3$. If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $12$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Using the algebraic difference quotient for a quadratic $q(x) = ax^2 + bx + d$ on $[1, c]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, c]} = \frac{q(c) - q(1)}{c - 1} = 2(c + 1) + 4$$
Setting this equal to $12$:
$$2(c + 1) + 4 = 12 \implies 2(c + 1) = 8 \implies c + 1 = 4 \implies c = 3$$

practiceQuestions.question:
**[2.8 (2.8.1) — Tabular Analysis #17]** Selected values of a function $f$ analyzed in *Inverse Functions* (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) are given in the table below:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 5 & 8 & 11 & 14 \\ \hline f(x) & 16 & 27 & 40 & 70 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
What is the average rate of change of $f$ over the closed interval $[5, 14]$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Using the average rate of change (difference quotient) formula over $[5, 14]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[5, 14]} = \frac{f(14) - f(5)}{14 - 5} = \frac{70 - 16}{9} = \frac{54}{9} = 6$$

**Exam Trap:** Do not stop after finding the net change $\Delta f = 54$ (which omits division by $\Delta x = 9$), and never invert the difference quotient as $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}$.

Which of the following statements about $g$ and its average rate of change over equal-length subintervals of $(4, 9)$ MUST be true?
choices: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.

(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.

practiceQuestions.explanation:
Because $g$ is decreasing on $(4, 9)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).

If $h(3) = 70$, what is the value of the parameter $k$, and what is the average rate of change of $h$ on $[0, 3]$?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
First solve for $k$ using $h(3) = 70$:
$$k(3)^2 + 7 = 70 \implies 9k = 63 \implies k = 7$$
Next, compute the average rate of change on $[0, 3]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,3]} = \frac{h(3) - h(0)}{3 - 0} = \frac{70 - 7}{3} = \frac{63}{3} = 21$$

practiceQuestions.stem: **[2.8 (2.8.1) — Calculator-Active Modeling #21]** A quantity studied in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) is modeled by the function $M(t) = 120(1.12)^t$ for $t \ge 0$ hours. practiceQuestions.question: **[2.8 (2.8.1) — Calculator-Active Modeling #21]** A quantity studied in **2.8: Inverse Functions** (*Inverse Functions — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) is modeled by the function $M(t) = 120(1.12)^t$ for $t \ge 0$ hours. Using a graphing calculator, what is the value of $M(5)$ and the average rate of change of $M$ over the interval $[0, 5]$, rounded to three decimal places?
practiceQuestions.explanation:
Evaluating $M(5)$ directly on a graphing calculator without intermediate rounding:
$$M(5) = 120(1.12)^{5} \approx 211.481$$
Since $M(0) = 120(1.12)^0 = 120$, the average rate of change on $[0, 5]$ is:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,5]} = \frac{M(5) - M(0)}{5 - 0} = \frac{211.481 - 120}{5} \approx 18.296$$

**Exam Trap:** Never assume $M(0) = 0$ for an exponential model $M(t) = a \cdot b^t$ (since $b^0 = 1$, $M(0) = 120$), and always divide the net change by $\Delta t = 5$.

To use the known value $f(2) = 4$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:

lesson.core_formula:
**Standard Exponential Function (Unit 2A REVIEW.1):**
$$f(x) = a \cdot b^x + k \quad (a \ne 0, b > 0, b \ne 1)$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** Horizontal asymptote at $y = k$; $y$-intercept at $(0, a + k)$.

**Point-Ratio Form Over Any Interval $[x_1, x_2]$ (Unit 2A REVIEW.1):**
$$y = y_1 \cdot \left(\frac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{\frac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1}}$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** Constructs an exponential function directly from two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$.

**Exponent-Base Manipulation Laws (Unit 2A REVIEW.1):**
$$b^{cx} = (b^c)^x, \quad b^{x + c} = b^c \cdot b^x$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** Demonstrates that horizontal dilations equal base changes, and horizontal shifts equal vertical stretches.
lesson.simple_explanation:
**Intuitive Analogy:** Think of exponential growth like a snowball rolling downhill that multiplies by the same factor $b$ on every equal step $\Delta x$, while a logarithm works in reverse by asking: "How many times did we multiply by base $b$ to reach this output?"

**How to Apply the Formula:**
1. **Growth vs. Decay and Concavity:** For $f(x) = a \cdot b^x$: if $a > 0$ and $b > 1$, $f$ exhibits **exponential growth** (increasing, concave up, $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = 0$). If $a > 0$ and $0 < b < 1$, $f$ exhibits **exponential decay** (decreasing, concave up, $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = 0$). If $a < 0$, the graph is reflected across the $x$-axis and is concave down.

**Quick Application Example:**
An exponential function $y = a \cdot b^x$ passes through $(1, 4)$ and $(3, 10)$. Find its equation and evaluate $y(5)$.
- Step 1: Over the interval $\Delta x = 3 - 1 = 2$, the output is multiplied by $\frac{10}{4} = 2.5$. Thus $b^2 = \frac{5}{2} \implies b = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}$.
- Step 2: Using point-ratio form from $(1, 4)$, $y = 4\left(\sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}\right)^{x - 1} = 4\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{\frac{x - 1}{2}}$.
- Step 3: At $x = 5$ (another step of $\Delta x = 2$ past $x = 3$), multiply $y(3) = 10$ by $2.5$: $y(5) = 10 \times 2.5 = 25$.

master_lesson.concept_description: Comprehensive synthesis and exam review for **Unit 2A - Exponential and Logarithmic Functions** (Sequences, exponential growth/manipulation, data modeling, model validation, compositions & inverses (Topics 2.1–2.8 + Review)). Consolidates all core formulas, rate-of-change analyses, graphical behaviors, and multi-step AP Free-Response justification strategies across Unit 2A. Mastering **Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW)** matters because it gives you the direct mathematical rule needed to set up, evaluate, and interpret AP Precalculus multiple-choice and free-response questions without guesswork.
master_lesson.core_formula:
**Standard Exponential Function (Unit 2A REVIEW.1):**
$$f(x) = a \cdot b^x + k \quad (a \ne 0, b > 0, b \ne 1)$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** Horizontal asymptote at $y = k$; $y$-intercept at $(0, a + k)$.

**Point-Ratio Form Over Any Interval $[x_1, x_2]$ (Unit 2A REVIEW.1):**
$$y = y_1 \cdot \left(\frac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{\frac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1}}$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** Constructs an exponential function directly from two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$.

**Exponent-Base Manipulation Laws (Unit 2A REVIEW.1):**
$$b^{cx} = (b^c)^x, \quad b^{x + c} = b^c \cdot b^x$$
- **Variables & Meaning:** Demonstrates that horizontal dilations equal base changes, and horizontal shifts equal vertical stretches.
master_lesson.simple_explanation:
**Intuitive Analogy:** Think of exponential growth like a snowball rolling downhill that multiplies by the same factor $b$ on every equal step $\Delta x$, while a logarithm works in reverse by asking: "How many times did we multiply by base $b$ to reach this output?"

**How to Apply the Formula:**
1. **Growth vs. Decay and Concavity:** For $f(x) = a \cdot b^x$: if $a > 0$ and $b > 1$, $f$ exhibits **exponential growth** (increasing, concave up, $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = 0$). If $a > 0$ and $0 < b < 1$, $f$ exhibits **exponential decay** (decreasing, concave up, $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = 0$). If $a < 0$, the graph is reflected across the $x$-axis and is concave down.

**Quick Application Example:**
An exponential function $y = a \cdot b^x$ passes through $(1, 4)$ and $(3, 10)$. Find its equation and evaluate $y(5)$.
- Step 1: Over the interval $\Delta x = 3 - 1 = 2$, the output is multiplied by $\frac{10}{4} = 2.5$. Thus $b^2 = \frac{5}{2} \implies b = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}$.
- Step 2: Using point-ratio form from $(1, 4)$, $y = 4\left(\sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}\right)^{x - 1} = 4\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{\frac{x - 1}{2}}$.
- Step 3: At $x = 5$ (another step of $\Delta x = 2$ past $x = 3$), multiply $y(3) = 10$ by $2.5$: $y(5) = 10 \times 2.5 = 25$.

mcq.question_latex: Let $f(x) = 3^x$ and $g(x) = 27 \cdot f(x)$. Which horizontal transformation of the graph of $f$ yields the exact same graph as $g$?
options: (A) A horizontal translation left by $3$ units
(B) A horizontal translation right by $3$ units
(C) A horizontal translation left by $27$ units
mcq.explanation_latex: Since $27 = 3^3$, we have $g(x) = 3^3 \cdot 3^x = 3^{x + 3} = f(x + 3)$, which is a horizontal translation left by $3$ units.
mcq.exam_trap: Confusing $3^{x+3}$ (shift left $3$) with $3^{3x} = 27^x$ (horizontal compression by $1/3$).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct Answer (A): Matches the governing AP Precalculus principle for Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW).
distractor_diagnostics.B: Selecting (B) A horizontal translation right by $3$ units triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Confusing $3^{x+3}$ (shift left $3$) with $3^{3x} = 27^x$ (horizontal compression by $1/3$).
distractor_diagnostics.C: Selecting (C) A horizontal translation left by $27$ units triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Confusing $3^{x+3}$ (shift left $3$) with $3^{3x} = 27^x$ (horizontal compression by $1/3$).
distractor_diagnostics.D: Selecting (D) A horizontal compression by factor $\frac{1}{3}$ triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Confusing $3^{x+3}$ (shift left $3$) with $3^{3x} = 27^x$ (horizontal compression by $1/3$).

mcq.question_latex: The function $f$ is increasing on $(-\infty, \infty)$ with selected values $(-2, 2), (-1, 6), (0, 18), (1, 54), (2, 162)$. Which statement properly justifies that $f$ is modeled by an exponential function?
options: (A) As input values increase by $1$, output values increase by a constant difference of $3$.
(B) Consecutive output values over equal-length input intervals are proportional with a constant ratio of $3$.
(C) The second differences of the outputs are constant.
(D) Input values are multiplied by $3$ while output values increase by $1$.
mcq.explanation_latex: Over equal input increments $\Delta x = 1$, the ratio of consecutive outputs is constant: $\frac{6}{2} = \frac{18}{6} = \frac{54}{18} = \frac{162}{54} = 3$. This proportional change over equal-length input intervals defines an exponential function.
mcq.exam_trap: Option (D) describes a logarithmic function, while Option (A) describes a linear function.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Selecting (A) As input values increase by $1$, output values increase by a constant difference of $3$. triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Option (D) describes a logarithmic function, while Option (A) describes a linear function.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Correct Answer (B): Matches the governing AP Precalculus principle for Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW).
distractor_diagnostics.C: Selecting (C) The second differences of the outputs are constant. triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Option (D) describes a logarithmic function, while Option (A) describes a linear function.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Selecting (D) Input values are multiplied by $3$ while output values increase by $1$. triggers a classic AP distractor trap: Option (D) describes a logarithmic function, while Option (A) describes a linear function.

mcq.question_latex:
**[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.1) — Tabular Analysis #1]** Selected values of a function $f$ analyzed in *Unit 2A REVIEW* (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) are given in the table below:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 1 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\ \hline f(x) & 3 & 9 & 17 & 33 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
What is the average rate of change of $f$ over the closed interval $[1, 7]$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Using the average rate of change (difference quotient) formula over $[1, 7]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, 7]} = \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = \frac{30}{6} = 5$$
mcq.exam_trap: Do not stop after finding the net change $\Delta f = 30$ (which omits division by $\Delta x = 6$), and never invert the difference quotient as $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y}$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Computed only the numerator net change $\Delta f = f(7) - f(1) = 33 - 3 = 30$ and forgot to divide by the interval width $\Delta x = 7 - 1 = 6$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the rate of change over the interior subinterval $[3, 5]$ ($\frac{17 - 9}{5 - 3} = 4$) instead of using the endpoints $x = 1$ and $x = 7$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Correct! Uses the difference quotient $\frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{33 - 3}{6} = 5$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Inverted the slope formula by computing $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} = \frac{6}{30} \approx 0.2$ instead of $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$.

mcq.question_latex: **[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.2) — Graphical Behavior #2]** On the open interval $(2, 7)$, the graph of a smooth function $g$ modeling *Unit 2A REVIEW* (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) is strictly decreasing and concave up. Which of the following statements about $g$ and its average rate of change over equal-length subintervals of $(2, 7)$ MUST be true?
options: (A) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and decreasing.
(B) The function values $g(x)$ are increasing, and the average rates of change are positive and decreasing.
(C) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the secant slopes are positive on every subinterval.
(D) The function values $g(x)$ are decreasing, and the average rates of change are negative and increasing.
mcq.explanation_latex: Because $g$ is decreasing on $(2, 7)$, its average rate of change is negative ($\frac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} < 0$). Because the graph of $g$ is **concave up**, its rates of change over equal-length subintervals are **strictly increasing** (becoming less negative, e.g., $-6, -3, -1$).
mcq.exam_trap: Confusing "negative and increasing" (e.g., $-6 < -3 < -1$, concave up) with "negative and becoming steeper" (which is decreasing, e.g., $-1 > -3 > -6$, concave down).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Looked at the magnitude of the negative slopes rather than their signed values. Moving from $-8$ to $-4$ to $-1$ is an INCREASING rate of change (concave up), whereas negative and decreasing ($-1, -4, -8$) is concave down.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Reversed the direction of $g(x)$. The prompt states $g$ is strictly decreasing.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Assumed "concave up" means positive slopes. A decreasing concave-up curve has negative slopes that are becoming less steep.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Decreasing function means negative rates of change, and concave up means the rates of change are increasing (becoming less negative, e.g., $-8, -4, -1$).

mcq.question_latex:
**[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.1) — Foundational Formula Use #3]** In the analysis of **Unit 2A REVIEW: Unit 2A REVIEW** (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*), the governing mathematical relationship is given by **Exponent-Base Manipulation Laws**:
$$b^{cx} = (b^c)^x, \quad b^{x + c} = b^c \cdot b^x$$
Which of the following best describes the mathematical role and domain condition of this identity?
options: (A) Demonstrates that horizontal dilations equal base changes, and horizontal shifts equal vertical stretches.
(B) It holds only when the average rate of change is identically zero over all real numbers.
(C) It requires the independent variable to be restricted exclusively to negative integers.
(D) It implies that the graph has a removable discontinuity (hole) at every integer input.
mcq.explanation_latex: By the AP Precalculus specifications for **Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.1)**, **Exponent-Base Manipulation Laws** ($b^{cx} = (b^c)^x, \quad b^{x + c} = b^c \cdot b^x$) satisfies: Demonstrates that horizontal dilations equal base changes, and horizontal shifts equal vertical stretches.
mcq.exam_trap: Overlooking explicit domain exclusions or confusing structural identities with constant-rate conditions.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct! Directly reflects the official AP Precalculus specification and domain condition for Exponent-Base Manipulation Laws in Unit 2A REVIEW.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Assumed a zero rate of change (constant function), which contradicts how Exponent-Base Manipulation Laws models dynamic covariation in Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Imposed an artificial negative-integer domain restriction not present in b^{cx} = (b^c)^x, \quad b^{x + c} = b^c \cdot b^x.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Confused standard functional evaluation in Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations with removable rational discontinuities (holes) at integer inputs.

mcq.question_latex: **[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.2) — Parameter Synthesis #4]** Let $h(x) = k x^2 + 6$ be a parameterized model studied in **Unit 2A REVIEW: Unit 2A REVIEW** (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*), where $k$ is a real constant. If $h(2) = 26$, what is the value of the parameter $k$, and what is the average rate of change of $h$ on $[0, 2]$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
First solve for $k$ using $h(2) = 26$:
$$k(2)^2 + 6 = 26 \implies 4k = 20 \implies k = 5$$
Next, compute the average rate of change on $[0, 2]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,2]} = \frac{h(2) - h(0)}{2 - 0} = \frac{26 - 6}{2} = \frac{20}{2} = 10$$
mcq.exam_trap: Forgetting to square the input $x = 2$ when solving $k(2)^2 = 20$, or forgetting to divide the net change $h(2) - h(0) = 20$ by the interval length $\Delta x = 2$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Found $k = 5$ correctly, but reported the net change $h(2) - h(0) = 20$ instead of dividing by the interval width $\Delta x = 2 - 0 = 2$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Correct! Isolating $k$ gives $k(2)^2 = 20 \implies k = 5$, and $\text{AROC}_{[0,2]} = \frac{26 - 6}{2 - 0} = 10$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Divided 20 by $2$ instead of $2^2 = 4$ when solving $k(2)^2 + 6 = 26$ for $k$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Forgot to divide by $2^2 = 4$ when isolating $k$, and used $h(2) = 26$ as the rate of change without subtracting $h(0) = 6$.

mcq.question_latex: **[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.1) — Calculator-Active Modeling #5]** A quantity studied in **Unit 2A REVIEW: Unit 2A REVIEW** (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) is modeled by the function $M(t) = 140(1.12)^t$ for $t \ge 0$ hours. Using a graphing calculator, what is the value of $M(4)$ and the average rate of change of $M$ over the interval $[0, 4]$, rounded to three decimal places?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Evaluating $M(4)$ directly on a graphing calculator without intermediate rounding:
$$M(4) = 140(1.12)^{4} \approx 220.293$$
Since $M(0) = 140(1.12)^0 = 140$, the average rate of change on $[0, 4]$ is:
$$\text{AROC}_{[0,4]} = \frac{M(4) - M(0)}{4 - 0} = \frac{220.293 - 140}{4} \approx 20.073$$
mcq.exam_trap: Never assume $M(0) = 0$ for an exponential model $M(t) = a \cdot b^t$ (since $b^0 = 1$, $M(0) = 140$), and always divide the net change by $\Delta t = 4$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Computed $M(4) \approx 220.293$ and subtracted $M(0) = 140$ to get $80.293$, but forgot to divide by the time interval $\Delta t = 4$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Treated the exponential power $(1.12)^{4}$ as multiplication 140 \cdot 1.12 \cdot 4 instead of exponentiation.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Divided $M(4)$ by $4$ without subtracting the initial value $M(0) = 140$ in the numerator (assuming $M(0) = 0$ when $(1.12)^0 = 1$).

mcq.question_latex: **[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.2) — Function Transformation #6]** Let $f$ be a parent function analyzed in **Unit 2A REVIEW: Unit 2A REVIEW** (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*) such that the point $(2, 3)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$. If $g(x) = 3f(x - 1) + 7$, which point must lie on the graph of $y = g(x)$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
To use the known value $f(2) = 3$, set the inner argument equal to $2$:
$$x - 1 = 2 \implies x = 2 + 1 = 3$$
Then evaluate the output $g(3)$:
$$g(3) = 3f(2) + 7 = 3(3) + 7 = 16$$
mcq.exam_trap: Inside horizontal transformations $f(x - h)$ act in the opposite direction of the sign ($x = x_0 + h$), and vertical stretches multiply $f(x)$ before adding the vertical translation $k$.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Subtracted $1$ from the $x$-coordinate instead of adding $1$. Remember that $f(x - 1)$ shifts the graph RIGHT by $1$ units ($x - 1 = 2 \implies x = 3$).
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Added the vertical shift $+7$ BEFORE multiplying by the vertical stretch factor $3$. By order of operations, multiply $3 \cdot 3$ first, then add $7$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Applied the vertical stretch factor $3$ to the $x$-coordinate instead of the $y$-coordinate.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Correct! Setting $x - 1 = 2$ gives $x = 3$ (horizontal shift right by $1$), and $g(3) = 3f(2) + 7 = 3(3) + 7 = 16$.

mcq.sub_topic_title: Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations
mcq.question_latex: **[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.1) — Secant Line Approximation #7]** A smooth, continuous function $p(x)$ studied in **Unit 2A REVIEW: Unit 2A REVIEW** (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) satisfies $p(3) = 5$ and $p(7) = 25$, and the graph of $p$ is strictly concave down on $[3, 7]$. Using the secant line connecting $(3, 5)$ and $(7, 25)$, what is the linear approximation for $p(4)$, and is it an overestimate or underestimate of the true value $p(4)$?
options: (A) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(B) The secant estimate is $10$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(C) The secant estimate is $25$, which is an underestimate because $p$ is concave down.
(D) The secant estimate is $15$, which is an overestimate because $p$ is concave down.
mcq.explanation_latex:
Step 1: Compute the slope of the secant line on $[3, 7]$:
$$m_{\text{sec}} = \frac{p(7) - p(3)}{7 - 3} = \frac{25 - 5}{4} = 5$$
Step 2: Evaluate the secant line equation at $x = 4$:
$$L(4) = p(3) + m_{\text{sec}}(4 - 3) = 5 + 5(1) = 10$$
Step 3: Because $p$ is **concave down** on $[3, 7]$, the graph arches above the straight secant line connecting the endpoints, so the secant line lies below the curve and produces an **underestimate**.
mcq.exam_trap: On a concave-down interval (arching like an umbrella), the straight secant line connecting two points lies BELOW the curve (underestimate), whereas on a concave-up interval (cupped upward) the secant line lies ABOVE the curve (overestimate).

distractor_diagnostics.A: Correct! The secant slope is $m = \frac{25 - 5}{7 - 3} = 5$, giving $L(4) = 5 + 5(4 - 3) = 10$. For a concave-down curve, the straight secant line connecting two points lies below the curve on $(3, 7)$, yielding an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Mistake: Computed the secant approximation $10$ properly, but reversed the concavity rule! Because a concave-down curve arches upward like an umbrella, the straight line connecting two points on the curve sits underneath the curve and gives an underestimate.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Used $L(x) = 5 + 5x$ instead of point-slope form $L(x) = 5 + 5(x - 3)$ (forgot to subtract $x_1 = 3$).
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Averaged the endpoint outputs $\frac{5 + 25}{2}$ even though $x = 4$ is not the midpoint of $[3, 7]$, and reversed the secant concavity inequality.

mcq.question_latex: **[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.2) — Score-5 Synthesis Challenge #8]** Let $q(x) = 3x^2 + 4x - 7$ be a function analyzed in **Unit 2A REVIEW: Unit 2A REVIEW** (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Graphical, Tabular & Contextual Modeling*, governed by *Growth vs. Decay and Concavity*). If the average rate of change of $q$ over the closed interval $[1, c]$ (where $c > 1$) is equal to $19$, what must be the value of the right endpoint $c$?
mcq.explanation_latex:
Using the algebraic difference quotient for a quadratic $q(x) = ax^2 + bx + d$ on $[1, c]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[1, c]} = \frac{q(c) - q(1)}{c - 1} = 3(c + 1) + 4$$
Setting this equal to $19$:
$$3(c + 1) + 4 = 19 \implies 3(c + 1) = 15 \implies c + 1 = 5 \implies c = 4$$
mcq.exam_trap: When factoring $\frac{c^2 - 1^2}{c - 1} = c + 1$, remember not to drop the linear term $+4$ or forget to subtract $1$ in the final step.

distractor_diagnostics.A: Mistake: Solved properly for $(1 + c) = 5$, but forgot to subtract the left endpoint $x_1 = 1$ to isolate $c$.
distractor_diagnostics.B: Correct! For $q(x) = 3x^2 + 4x - 7$, the difference quotient on $[1, c]$ simplifies to $\text{AROC} = 3(1 + c) + 4$. Setting 3(1 + c) + 4 = 19 yields $c = 4$.
distractor_diagnostics.C: Mistake: Subtracted the linear coefficient $4$ from $19$, but forgot to divide by the leading coefficient $a = 3$ and subtract $1$.
distractor_diagnostics.D: Mistake: Confused the average rate of change with the total change $q(4) - q(1) = 57$.

**[Unit 2A REVIEW (Unit 2A REVIEW.1) — Tabular Analysis #9]** Selected values of a function $f$ analyzed in *Unit 2A REVIEW* (*Unit 2A REVIEW — Core Algebraic & Analytical Foundations*) are given in the table below:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 3 & 7 & 11 & 15 \\ \hline f(x) & 16 & 38 & 62 & 112 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
What is the average rate of change of $f$ over the closed interval $[3, 15]$?

Using the average rate of change (difference quotient) formula over $[3, 15]$:
$$\text{AROC}_{[3, 15]} = \frac{f(15) - f(3)}{15 - 3} = \frac{112 - 16}{12} = \frac{96}{12} = 8$$
